Early repeat requests fell from 17 percent to 6 percent of HbA1c requests over 12 months. Clinicians overrode 4.3 percent of held requests, most often for pregnancy or a recent change in treatment. A review of 200 held requests found no case in which the hold delayed a treatment decision judged important by two diabetologists. Requesters complained mainly about the wording of the comment in the first two months after the rule started."},{"title":"Minimum retesting intervals in clinical biochemistry: a consensus statement","authors":"Laboratory Test Utilisation Working Group","year":2016,"venue":"Clinical Biochemistry Practice Statements","providerType":"guideline","abstract":"A working group of laboratory professionals and clinicians agreed minimum retesting intervals for 24 common tests. For HbA1c, three months was agreed for monitoring established diabetes, with exceptions for pregnancy, suspected rapid change, new diagnosis and conditions affecting red cell turnover. The group advised that any hold rule must offer a simple override and that laboratories should review held requests for harm. Evidence for most intervals was indirect, and the statement relied on expert agreement for 19 of the 24 tests."},{"title":"Why clinicians repeat HbA1c early: an analysis of override reasons under an interval rule","authors":"Tanaka-Obi R, Halvorsen-Adeyemi S","year":2022,"venue":"Primary Care Laboratory Medicine","doi":"10.5555/pclm.2022.0110","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Across 18 practices using an interval rule, 1,905 held HbA1c requests were followed. Requesters overrode 212 (11.1 percent); the reason matched an accepted exception in 58 percent of overrides, and in the rest the most common reason was a patient appointment already booked. The median time from hold to override was 1 working day. Practices with a named diabetes nurse overrode less often. Overrides without an accepted reason clustered among a few clinicians, which suggests that feedback could be targeted."},{"title":"Acceptability of laboratory demand management rules among primary care clinicians","authors":"Ferreira-Lindgren M, Achebe-Nakamura J, Brandt-Oduya P","year":2024,"venue":"Primary Care Laboratory Medicine","doi":"10.5555/pclm.2024.0037","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We surveyed 312 primary care clinicians and held group discussions with 26 in practices that had used laboratory hold rules for at least a year. Most accepted hold rules for tests they saw as low risk, but 39 percent felt that rules on diabetes monitoring interfered with their clinical judgement. Acceptance was higher when the comment explained the reason in one sentence and gave the override route. Clinicians wanted the rule to recognise pregnancy and recent treatment changes automatically where the record allowed it."},{"title":"Concentration of early repeat HbA1c testing among primary care practices: implications for targeting","authors":"Quist-Mbeki A, Sorensen-Reid T","year":2020,"venue":"Laboratory Utilisation Reports","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using two years of laboratory data from 70 practices, we found that the 10 percent of practices with the most early repeat HbA1c requests accounted for 38 percent of all early repeats. Early repeats were more common where results were requested by practice-based pharmacists and in practices with high locum use. Practices whose recall systems booked diabetes reviews at fixed three-month intervals also had more early repeats. Targeting feedback to high-repeat practices reduced early repeats by a third in a small follow-up. The analysis could not examine individual clinical reasons for repeat requests."}]}
